title: Drop by drop
hook: as a water jar fills drop by drop, so goodness gathers little by little (Dhammapada 122)
tomorrow: what made the Buddha stop a fight between two groups of monks?

segments.voice: A week of verses, six lines so far. The path, with the mind first. Earnest, the Buddha's last word of advice. My own list. The solid rock in praise and blame. One word of peace. Conquer myself. Zoe and Theo had their coffee. It went better than her three points would have.

segments.voice: A leaky faucet at night: one drop, then another, and by morning the glass under it is full. That's the whole answer to how a jar fills from a tap that only drips. Verse one twenty-two, in Max Müller's translation: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The verse is about goodness. And its story starts with a rich man who gave almost nothing.
screen: `A LEAKY FAUCET, A FULL GLASS.` → `A WATER-POT FILLED BY DROPS.` → `A RICH MAN WHO GAVE ALMOST NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The commentary tells it. A man in Savatthi went door to door gathering food so the whole town could offer one meal to the Buddha and his monks. At a rich man's house he was given a pinch of rice, a drop of butter, a little honey: a gift so small it was nearly an insult. He didn't sneer. He mixed those few grains into the big pots with everyone else's, and wished the rich man well for his share. The rich man had come to watch, expecting to be mocked. He heard the blessing instead, and asked forgiveness. The Buddha spoke the verse: don't think lightly of good, saying it won't come to me; drop by drop the pot fills, and the wise fill up with good little by little. Buddhists call what gathers that way merit, punna in Pali, and many make it in small daily acts: a spoonful of rice in a monk's bowl, a flower at a shrine, a kind word, often dedicated to others. The verse's own point: no good is too small to count. Drop by drop.
screen: `DOOR TO DOOR FOR ONE MEAL.` · `A PINCH OF RICE, MIXED IN ANYWAY.` · `DROP BY DROP THE POT FILLS.` · `MERIT, MADE IN SMALL ACTS.` · then, large: `DROP BY DROP.`

segments.voice: Count small good things from this week, one for each breath: a door held, a text answered, a cup of tea someone made. Let each one fall like a drop. Don't hunt for big ones; the small ones are the point.
Drop by drop: goodness gathered little by little, the way a water-pot fills from a dripping tap.
Your line: drop by drop, and no drop too small. One week inside the Dhammapada, seven lines in the jar.

howItsDone: Buddhists speak of making merit (punna) through small, regular acts: giving food to monks on their alms round, offering flowers or light at a shrine, keeping precepts, and dedicating the merit to others.
